# Parley v0.1.34

A permission profile's execution rule now reaches Claude. If you use a profile
that restricts running tools or processes — Default, Flexible and Workspace
folders all do — expect a permission prompt where an agent previously ran a
shell command without asking.

## Execution rules are no longer dropped

A permission profile describes ten capabilities. Until now Parley translated
exactly one of them into a vendor launch: whether the agent may write in the
project. The rest were recorded, shown in the permission review, and never
reached the CLI.

That had a visible consequence. Allowing project writes selects Claude's
`acceptEdits` mode, and that mode auto-approves file edits plus a set of
filesystem shell commands — `mkdir`, `touch`, `rm`, `mv`, `cp` and others. A
profile could say execution requires approval and an agent would still run
those commands unprompted.

The reason was a mismatch in shape rather than an oversight: a permission mode
is a single setting, and a profile has separate rules for writing and for
execution. There is no mode meaning "accept edits but ask before commands".

Parley now sends the execution rule as a permission rule instead of folding it
into the mode. A profile requiring approval asks before a shell command; a
profile denying execution blocks it. Both take precedence over the permission
mode, so the profile you chose is what applies.

Nothing changes for a profile that allows execution, including Broad workspace.

**Bypass is untouched.** If you selected Bypass vendor permissions for a
container, no rule is sent at all. That choice is yours to make and Parley does
not quietly reverse it.

## The review says what it does and does not carry

Where a rule cannot be expressed to a vendor, the permission review now names
the restricted capabilities in plain words and says they are not translated
into a launch argument. Where it can be expressed, it says the restriction is
carried and takes precedence over the permission mode. Previously the review
showed rules without indicating which ones reached the CLI at all.

## Internal work

The parts of the core that describe a handoff no longer depend on the code that
delivers one. A handoff record, a reviewed command run, a container's Git
identity and a permission selection can each be read without the machinery
behind them. This is preparation and changes no behaviour.

A repository check now records which core files depend on Apple frameworks and
fails if that set changes in either direction, so the platform-free majority
cannot quietly acquire a dependency, and progress cannot go unrecorded.

There is also a new guide for building container images, covering the exact
utilities an image must provide, the conditions it must tolerate, worked
Dockerfiles and a command to check any image before relying on it.

## Compatibility

Agent protocol is unchanged at 32. A pane started on an earlier build keeps
that build's behaviour until it is restarted, so restart panes to pick up the
permission change.

Validated: 332 native checks, 53 Node tests, public scan, platform scan and
build. The execution rule was confirmed present in the launch arguments of
running host and container panes, and confirmed to block a shell command in a
non-interactive session. Whether an interactive session shows a prompt has not
been observed and is the reason this build exists.

Unnotarized test beta: ad-hoc signed without the hardened runtime, not
notarized, no automatic updates. Install only from the expected GitLab
release after checking SHA256SUMS.
